title: In the original, the A did not mean Achievable. It meant Assignable: who is actually going to do it.
description:
consultant and former corporate planning director at Washington Water Power, writing in Spokane

In the original, the A did not mean Achievable. It meant Assignable: who is actually going to do it. Doran's five were Specific, Measurable, Assignable, Realistic and Time-related. Achievable and Relevant came later.

the length of the Management Review article that introduced SMART, pages 35 and 36 of the November 1981 issue.

Doran wrote that the acronym does not mean every objective will have all five criteria. Many people still assume all five are compulsory.

Researchers reviewing its use in physical activity programmes have pointed out it was never built on theory or experimental evidence. It began as advice for managers writing objectives, not as a tested method.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMART_criteria: confirms the acronym was first proposed by George T. Doran in the November 1981 issue of Management Review (vol. 70, issue 11, pp. 35 to 36), in a paper titled 'There's a S.M.A.R.T. way to write management's goals and objectives'; that his original letters stood for Specific, Measurable, Assignable, Realistic and Time-related; that 'achievable' and 'relevant' are later substitutions; that SMART is linked to, not written by, Peter Drucker's management by objectives; and that Swann and colleagues criticise the framework's lack of theoretical or empirical foundation.
- https://www.projectsmart.co.uk/smart-goals/brief-history-of-smart-goals.php: confirms Doran was a consultant and former Director of Corporate Planning for Washington Water Power Company, writing in Spokane, Washington; quotes his line that the acronym 'doesn't mean that every objective written will have all five criteria'; and notes his son Sean Doran confirmed the attribution to the site.
